new_paragraphs: According to general system architecture, interaction control logic defines the procedures through which the user interacts with the High Power Laser VL8 device. It coordinates with the control software to respond to user inputs and determines the content and timing of information and feedback presented to the user.

Drivers for input devices are responsible for detecting user actions on input devices, such as press/release of buttons and touch events on the touchscreen. The Input interpreter handles complex user input events, such as long-press actions on input widgets, mapping between touchscreen coordinates and input widgets, and continuous user actions such as handswitch actuation. Output render defines how feedback is presented to the user. Drivers for output devices command output devices (e.g., display, speakers) to present feedback to the user. The High Power Laser VL8 device has two pieces of software. Driver software tasks are to control and adjust the device's output. GUI software provides a Graphical User Interface (GUI) between user and the device. Communication between GUI and Driver software is fulfilled through serial communication protocol (RS-232). The device supports a maximum output power of 8 watts, which can be fully generated by either the 1064 nm or 808 nm diode.

new_paragraphs:
1. LCD Module
The GUI software generates the data to be displayed on the 7-inch touch LCD, which can include text, images, icons, and other graphical elements. The user can view and interact with the information presented on the screen. The GUI software receives user input from the integrated touch panel (Vertical ITF In-Cell Touch Framework). It interprets the touch coordinates and performs appropriate actions based on the user's interaction.

2. Sound Module
The GUI software processes user input data to determine the desired volume levels for touch feedback and alarm tones. Once the desired volume levels are determined, the GUI software sends the corresponding data to the sound module of the device. Users can select different alarm tones and adjust alarm volume through the Settings page.

3. Wi-Fi Module
The GUI software communicates with a remote server to determine if any software updates are available for the device. If an update is available, it downloads the update package from the server. Once the user confirms the update, the GUI software initiates the update process and manages the transfer of the update package to the device via the Wi-Fi module. Network time synchronization is also available through this module.

4. Storage Flash Memory
To save therapeutic protocols, user-defined programs, favorites, placement images, error messages and other user settings, a storage flash memory (MicroSD card) is used.

5. Battery
The microcontroller continuously monitors the battery voltage level using the ADC. It compares the voltage against predefined thresholds that indicate the battery's state of charge or health. If the battery voltage drops below a specific threshold (20%), the microcontroller generates a low battery warning visible on the GUI. The microcontroller also implements battery protection mechanisms to safeguard against overcharging or deep discharging. It controls the charging circuits to regulate the charging process and protect the battery's integrity. A visual notification is displayed on the UI when the charger is connected.

6. Temperature Sensor
Temperature sensors with nonlinear (exponential) output characteristics are used. One sensor measures the laser diode temperature and another controls the temperature of the device battery. These measurements are sent to the Driver's Microcontroller to control the fans and output laser. If the laser module exceeds 35°C, an immediate emission interruption is triggered.

new_paragraphs:
7. Fiber Sensor
This sensor is able to recognize if the optic fiber (handpiece fiber cable) is not connected to the device. This data is sent to the Driver's Microcontroller and then to the GUI Module to warn the user, preventing laser emission until the fiber is properly connected.

8. Handswitch
The Microcontroller controls the Handswitch state (pressed or released). If the handswitch is connected, the Microcontroller waits for pressing its switch to start applying the output laser. The sensor also detects if the handswitch is not connected, sending this data to the Driver's Microcontroller and then to the GUI Module to warn the user. The switch mode (Toggle or Momentary) is configurable from the Settings page.

9. LED
The device includes an LED that indicates the status of the laser radiation module. The microcontroller controls the LED, allowing it to change colors to represent four different modes: off, standby, ready, and emitting. A red indicator light is activated when the laser starts running.

10. Cooling System
By controlling the cooling system including TEC and Fan through the microcontroller, the High Power Laser VL8 device effectively regulates its temperature, providing optimal performance and preventing overheating. The microcontroller controls the operation of the Thermoelectric Cooler (TEC) and can adjust the power supplied to regulate device temperature. In addition, the microcontroller controls the fan speed to increase or decrease airflow.

11. Interlock
The driver software constantly monitors the status of the interlock. The interlock is configurable from the Settings > Security page, where the user can enable or disable the requirement of a remote interlock for running output. When active, the device remains locked until the interlock condition is satisfied. The GUI displays a yellow warning indicator when the interlock is not connected.

12. Laser Module
The High Power Laser VL8 device is equipped with a laser driver circuit that provides the necessary electrical power and control signals to the laser module. The device supports two laser diodes operating at 808 nm and 1064 nm wavelengths, each capable of delivering up to 8 watts of peak power. Users can distribute the output power between both wavelengths based on treatment requirements. The laser driver circuit is connected to the microcontroller.
13. Aiming Beam Controller

Error command (e.g., Fiber or Handswitch Disconnection command)
Handswitch state (Pressed or Released)
Temperature (laser diode and battery)
Battery State and charge percentage

2.1. Therapy Parameters
All relevant settings and parameters for the laser therapy session are clearly displayed and easily adjustable on this page.
Therapy Modes: Five modes are available — Continuous Wave (CW), Pulsed, and others. In CW mode, Frequency and Duty Cycle settings are automatically disabled. Different modes can be set for each wavelength independently.
Output Mode Options (one selectable at a time):
Timer Option: Users manually set the Time parameter; Energy is calculated automatically based on set time.
Dose Option: Users set Dose (J/cm²) and Area (cm²); Time (min) and Energy (Joule) are calculated automatically.
Time: Adjustable from 1 minute to 60 minutes with a step of 1 minute.
Wavelength Selection and Peak Power:
808 nm: 0 W to 8 W
1064 nm: 0 W to 8 W
Combined Mode (Both Wavelengths): 0.1 W to 8 W total power distribution between both sources
Duty Cycle: Adjustable from 5% to 100% in 5% increments.
Frequency: Selectable from 1 Hz to 1 kHz (step of 1 for 1–10 Hz, 5 for 10–100 Hz, 50 for 100–1000 Hz).
Area: Ranges from 1 cm² to 225 cm²; increasing area increases treatment time and total Energy.
Dose: Ranges from 1 J/cm² to 100 J/cm²; increasing Dose increases treatment time and total Energy.
